title: Active Curriculum Refinement for Reinforcement Learning
claim: Modeling the environment space as an explicit graph lets adaptive path sampling cover and master all nodes more efficiently than random exploration.
layout: 5 panels, left-to-right, same graph recolored per stage (white→yellow/blue→purple→all blue)
description: Five panels in a row. Panel (a) is a plain teal square labeled Θ, followed by an equals sign linking it to panel (b), a rounded mint box holding a directed acyclic graph of white nodes with arrows branching left to right, and ellipses at the edges to show the graph continues. Panel (c) shows the same graph with yellow arrows tracing random paths. Visited nodes are blue, and nodes learned by generalization are yellow. The rest stay white. Panel (d) shows purple arrows and purple nodes fanning out from one chosen node, which stands for targeted active resampling. Panel (e) shows every node blue, meaning the whole graph is learned. The eye goes first to the color changes from white to blue, yellow and purple across the repeated graph. Panels are labeled (a) to (e) underneath.
caption: Overview of PATH. (a) A environment distribution Θ. (b) The same space viewed as an explicit curriculum DAG G, where edges encode prerequisite relations between environments. (c) PATH:RANDOM explores G by sampling random paths (yellow trajectories); blue nodes are explicitly visited and learned, while yellow nodes denote additional environments learned via generalization from nearby visited nodes. (d) PATH:ACTIVE identifies a node with high learning potential, then it allocates more sampling by launching multiple random paths (purple) from that node. (e) This adaptive allocation rapidly increases coverage and efficient learns all nodes in G.
abstract: In many reinforcement learning (RL) domains, environments are connected by prerequisite relations, such as difficulty-increasing edits or parameter increments, which induce a directed acyclic curriculum graph (DAG). Although this structure is often exploited only implicitly, explicitly modeling it can improve training. We introduce PATH, a curriculum-learning framework that performs active learning over the curriculum graph. PATH first expands coverage by sampling diverse curriculum paths and then reallocates training toward regions that remain unmastered. Experiments across diverse environments show that PATH explicitly leverages the graph structure to achieve strong robustness and generalization.
